recipe: Use a build script to manually link stdc++ when your foreign library is a C++ static library that exposes a C interface.
trigger_condition: When the foreign library is a C++ static library with a C interface and stdc++ is not linked by default.
evidence: The easiest way to do this is by setting up a build script.

recipe: Wrap calls to foreign functions in `unsafe {}` blocks, as foreign functions are assumed unsafe.
trigger_condition: When calling any function declared in an `extern "C"` block.
evidence: Foreign functions are assumed to be unsafe so calls to them need to be wrapped with unsafe {} as a promise to the compiler that everything contained within truly is safe.

recipe: Carefully specify argument types for foreign functions, since the Rust compiler cannot verify correctness at compile time.
trigger_condition: When declaring the signature of a foreign function in an extern block.
evidence: When declaring the argument types to a foreign function, the Rust compiler cannot check if the declaration is correct, so specifying it correctly is part of keeping the binding correct at runtime.

recipe: Wrap raw C API functions with safe, high-level Rust functions that accept slices and return owned types like Vec, hiding the unsafe internals from the public API.
trigger_condition: When exposing a foreign library's API to Rust users.
evidence: The raw C API needs to be wrapped to provide memory safety and make use of higher-level concepts like vectors. A library can choose to expose only the safe, high-level interface and hide the unsafe internal details.

recipe: After a foreign function writes to an output buffer and reports the actual length, call `set_len()` on the vector to reflect the true content size.
trigger_condition: When a foreign function writes to an output buffer and returns the resulting length via a pointer argument.
evidence: An output parameter is also passed to retrieve the true length after compression for setting the length.

recipe: Use Rust's Drop trait (destructors) to release resources handed off by foreign libraries, ensuring cleanup happens even on panic.
trigger_condition: When a foreign library transfers ownership of a resource to your Rust code.
evidence: Foreign libraries often hand off ownership of resources to the calling code.

recipe: When an external library spawns its own threads and invokes callbacks, use synchronization mechanisms (mutexes or channels in std::sync::mpsp) to safely access Rust data structures from the callback.
trigger_condition: An external C library spawns its own threads and invokes callbacks from those threads.
evidence: In these cases access to Rust data structures inside the callbacks is especially unsafe and proper synchronization mechanisms must be used.

recipe: For native C/C++ build dependencies that are not distributed as libraries, archive the code into a static library and declare the dependency with #[link(name = "foo", kind = "static")].
trigger_condition: You need C/C++ glue code for a Rust crate but don't want to distribute the native code separately.
evidence: the native static library will be included in the output, meaning that distribution of the native static library is not necessary.

recipe: Use CString from std::ffi when you need a NUL-terminated string for C interoperability, since Rust strings are not NUL-terminated.
trigger_condition: A C API expects a NUL-terminated string and you have a Rust String to pass.
evidence: If you need a NUL-terminated string for interoperability with C, you should use the CString type in the std::ffi module.

recipe: Declare variadic foreign functions by specifying ... within the argument list of the extern block, since normal Rust functions cannot be variadic.

recipe: Represent nullable C pointers using Option<T> where T is a non-nullable Rust type (references, Box<T>, or function pointers), as this is guaranteed to work with the C ABI via the nullable pointer optimization.
trigger_condition: A C API uses pointers that may be null and you need to represent them in Rust without transmutes.
evidence: The most common type that takes advantage of the nullable pointer optimization is Option<T>, where None corresponds to null.

recipe: Use the -unwind variant of the ABI string when you expect Rust panics or foreign exceptions to cross an FFI boundary; use the non-unwind variant when you do not.
trigger_condition: You are defining an FFI boundary and need to decide whether unwinding should be allowed across it.
evidence: If you expect Rust panics or foreign (e.g. C++) exceptions to cross an FFI boundary, that boundary must use the appropriate -unwind ABI string.

recipe: Add #[repr(C)] to any custom struct you intend to use in FFI.
trigger_condition: You are defining a Rust struct to serve as an opaque type in foreign function interface code.
evidence: We also want to use this type in FFI, so we have to add #[repr(C)].

recipe: Include a marker field (e.g., PhantomData<(*mut u8, PhantomPinned)>) to prevent the compiler from auto-deriving Send, Sync, and Unpin on your opaque struct.
trigger_condition: Your opaque FFI struct wraps a pointer and you want to control its trait bounds explicitly.
evidence: The marker ensures the compiler does not mark the struct as Send, Sync, and Unpin. (*mut u8 is not Send or Sync, PhantomPinned is not Unpin)

recipe: Avoid using an empty enum as an FFI type, because the compiler relies on empty enums being uninhabited and handling values of type &Empty can trigger undefined behavior.
trigger_condition: You are choosing a Rust type to represent an opaque C type in FFI and considering an empty enum.
evidence: Notice that it is a really bad idea to use an empty enum as FFI type.
